Lark bunting (Calamospiza melanocorys) females construct open cup nests on the ground in mixed-grass prairie habitats across the Great Plains. Field studies have documented that freshly laid clutches consist of three to seven eggs [N_R_i = clutches consist of three to seven eggs], a relatively modest brood size characteristic of many icterid songbirds occupying unpredictable environments. Under controlled incubation conditions maintained at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the incubation period spans approximately 12 days [ab = approximately 12 days], culminating in the hatching of altricial nestlings. These chicks emerge extremely underdeveloped, weighing just 3.28 grams [Wwb = 3.28 grams] at the moment of hatching, a neonatal mass that represents a small fraction of the eventual adult body size. The initial mass of the freshly laid egg, reflecting the resources provisioned by the female prior to laying, has been measured at 3.14 grams [Ww0 = 3.14 grams], indicating that the egg undergoes minimal mass change during incubation before the chick emerges.

The post-hatching development of the altricial nestling proceeds rapidly under the sustained provisioning efforts of both parents. Under the thermal regime characteristic of the breeding season, where adults maintain nest temperatures around 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the young achieve the capacity for sustained flight at 8.5 days after hatching [tx = 8.5 days after hatching]. This abbreviated nestling period is unusually short compared to many temperate passerines, presumably an adaptation to the ephemeral nature of prairie insect emergence and the risk of nest predation. Following fledging, the juveniles continue to receive parental care for a brief period before attaining nutritional independence. The reproductive strategy of this species appears geared toward maximizing seasonal output under favorable conditions, as females can initiate subsequent nesting attempts rapidly if an earlier attempt is successful or, more commonly, if it fails to predation.

Sexual maturation in the lark bunting occurs relatively quickly for a bird of its body size, with individuals reaching puberty at 25.5 days after hatching [tp = 25.5 days after hatching] under the warm conditions typical of the breeding grounds where ambient temperatures approximate 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This remarkably early onset of gonadal maturity allows young males, still in their juvenal plumage, to begin establishing territories late in the same breeding season in which they hatched, though most individuals do not actually breed until the following year. The first successful brood for a typical female, measured as the time since birth at first reproduction, occurs approximately 365 days after hatching [tR = approximately 365 days after hatching], aligning with the return to the breeding grounds at o at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]ne year of age. This interval between hatching and first breeding allows for complete somatic growth, the acquisition of adult plumage, and the accumulation of sufficient endogenous reserves to support egg production and incubation.

Adult body mass in Calamospiza melanocorys exhibits considerable sexual size dimorphism, a pattern common among polygynous passerines. When considering the ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown adults, females typically reach an asymptotic mass of 23.6 grams [Wwi = 23.6 grams], whereas males, which are larger and more conspicuously ornamented during the breeding season, achieve a significantly higher ultimate wet weight of 36.1 grams [Wwi = 36.1 grams]. This roughly fifty percent disparity in mass reflects the intense sexual selection pressures operating on male body size in a lek-like mating system where larger individuals hold superior territories. The 12.5 gram difference between the sexes also has implications for foraging ecology, as males may be able to exploit larger prey items or defend richer feeding patches. Energetic demands during the brief breeding season are considerable, especially for females producing multiple clutches while also thermoregulating the developing embryos.

The lifespan of the lark bunting, based on field records from mark-recapture studies conducted across its core breeding range, indicates a maximum longevity of approximately 4.8 years [am = approximately 4.8 years] under natural conditions, with individuals experiencing the active metabolic temperatures characteristic of summer on the shortgrass prairie, around 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively short lifespan, comparable to many other small-bodied grassland passerines, imposes significant demographic constraints on lifetime reproductive output. Females that survive multiple breeding seasons can produce three to seven eggs per clutch [N_R_i = three to seven eggs per clutch] and typically attempt approximately 1.5 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 1.5 clutches per year], though the exact number of clutches attempted annually is highly variable. The combination of a modest clutch size and a brief maximum lifespan underscores the importance of high annual nesting success for population persistence. Marked population fluctuations, driven by variation in rainfall and concomitant insect abundance on the breeding grounds, further complicate the demography of this obligate grassland specialist.
